newsitem.title: GREECE: GREECE DOWNGRADES EXPERTS' COMMITTEE WITH TURKEY.
newsitem.headline: GREECE DOWNGRADES EXPERTS' COMMITTEE WITH TURKEY.

text.p: Greece, which almost clashed with neighbouring Turkey last year, said on Wednesday a group of experts from both countries that was supposed to help resolve thorny differences would not actually meet face-to-face.

Athens had proposed earlier this month setting up an experts' committee from both countries to discuss procedural issues relating to Greek-Turkish disputes, which have long soured relations between the two NATO members.
"There will not be joint meeting between the teams of experts," Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos told a news conference.
He said the two groups would communicate through the Dutch presidency of the European Union, which has been trying to mediate between the feuding countries.

The prospect of talks with Turkey angered many within Greece's ruling socialist party and 32 deputies signed an open letter to the government last week, warning against getting too close with Turkey while contentious issues remained unresolved.

The government has refused to comment on the letter, saying it was an internal party affair but political analysts said it made clear not all socialists shared technocrat Prime Minister Costas Simitis' vision of rapprochement with Turkey.
Athens and Ankara have long been at odds over territorial differences in the Aegean Sea, minorities in both countries and the divided island of Cyprus.
EU-member Greece has blocked Turkey's efforts to get closer to the 15-member bloc, citing what it sees as aggression from Ankara and a poor human rights record.

Cyprus, which also wants to join the EU, has been divided since 1974 when Turkish troops invaded and occupied it northern third after a coup attempt in Nicosia engineered by a military junta then ruling Greece.

The EU was delighted to see the first signs of rapprochement last week when Greek deputy foreign minister George Papandreou met his Turkish counterpart Onur Oymen on the fringes of a Malta conference, where the EU initiative was put on the table.
"A breakthrough took place today and we shall see the results in the future," Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said after the meeting.

It was the first time the two NATO allies have considered talking since January last year when they almost clashed over two uninhabited islets in the eastern Aegean Sea. War was averted with last-minute U.S. intervention.

Ankara has repeatedly called for direct dialogue to resolve differences. Athens has adamantly rejected this, saying it would never negotiate its borders, and wants Turkey to take its territorial claims to the International Court at the Hague.
Pangalos clarified on Wednesday the two countries were nowhere near a breakthrough.
"A overall territorial claim cannot be settled by bargaining. It would inevitably lead to a clash, which is something we don't want," he said.
He said real progress can only be made if Turkey abandons its threats of war against Greece and takes its territorial demands to international mediation. --Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
